subject: system-design
title: Distributed Messaging Queue
summary: An asynchronous buffer that decouples producers from consumers, smooths traffic spikes, and lets work survive a slow or crashed worker.

blocks.text: A message queue sits between a producer that creates work and a consumer that does it. Instead of calling the consumer directly, the producer drops a message on the queue and moves on; the consumer pulls messages and processes them at its own pace. That asynchronous buffer is what decouples the two sides.

items: Absorbs spikes: a burst of work queues up instead of overwhelming the consumer (backpressure).
Resilience: if a consumer crashes, messages wait in the queue rather than being lost.
Independence: producers and consumers can scale, deploy, and fail separately.

blocks.text: A classic queue is point-to-point: each message is delivered to exactly one consumer. The queue is a unit of work to be done once — process a payment, resize an image — not a broadcast, which is the distinction from pub-sub, where every subscriber gets a copy. But delivery across a network is never free, so queues offer different guarantees:

items: At-most-once: a message may be lost but never processed twice.
At-least-once: never lost, but may be delivered more than once.
Exactly-once: processed once and only once — the ideal, and the hardest.

blocks.title: The practical choice
blocks.text: Exactly-once is hard because the network fails at the worst moment — a consumer may finish the work but crash before acknowledging, so the queue redelivers. Most systems instead pick at-least-once and make consumers idempotent: processing the same message twice has the same effect as once.

Strict global ordering is expensive, so many queues guarantee order only within a partition or key, not across the whole queue. Delivery works on acks and a visibility timeout: a pulled message is hidden from other consumers for a window, and if it isn't acknowledged in time it reappears and is redelivered — exactly why consumers must be idempotent.

To go faster, run many consumers as a group and split the messages among them, so throughput scales with the number of workers. Each message still goes to only one consumer in the group, preserving point-to-point delivery while parallelizing the work.

Kafka is a partitioned, high-throughput log that keeps messages so consumers can replay them; SQS is a managed cloud queue that hides the operational work; RabbitMQ is a flexible broker with rich routing. They differ in throughput, ordering, and retention, but all give you the same core decoupling.
